growth_story.headline: Saudi Arabia's income per person is still 58.2 percent below its 1974 oil-boom peak; since 2003 it has grown 1.1 percent a year, still swinging with oil.
growth_story.arc: Saudi Arabia's income per person peaked in 1974, during the oil boom, and is still 58.2 percent below that peak, about where it first stood in 1968. The IMF links the collapse of the early 1980s to falling oil prices, which cut oil output and pushed growth below zero. From 1990 to 2002 income per person fell by 1.6 percent a year: the IMF describes comparatively steady growth in total output after the 1980s, but the population grew quickly. Since 2003 it has grown by 1.1 percent a year, first on rising oil prices and production, then, after oil prices fell in 2014, with a push to grow the non-oil economy under the Vision 2030 reforms. Growth stayed uneven: it averaged 0.7 percent a year over 2006–2015 and 0.9 percent over 2016–2025, with a fall of 8.3 percent in 2020, gains of 9.2 and 7.2 percent in 2021 and 2022, and a decline in each year from 2023 to 2025, as cuts to oil output weighed on growth in 2023 and 2024.

threads.title: The oil bust of the 1980s
threads.text: Income per person reached its peak in 1974. When oil prices fell in the early 1980s, Saudi oil output fell sharply and the economy shrank; income per person fell by 21.1 percent in 1982 alone.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe strong growth in total output in 2025, as OPEC+ cuts were unwound, yet in the data income per person fell by 0.2 percent that year and has fallen in each year since 2022. The same gap shows up after 1990: the IMF describes comparatively steady output growth, while income per person fell by 1.6 percent a year from 1990 to 2002. The IMF points to the rapid increase in population for the earlier gap, but the recent sources do not say how much of the recent gap it explains.
